### The Hook: Dr. Chen's Dilemma

Dr. Mei Chen, a postdoc at a top-20 computer science department, stares at two browser tabs open side by side. The first shows the NeurIPS 2025 main track Call for Papers. Its language is unmistakable: the track seeks "new algorithms, theoretical foundations, and novel methods" for machine learning. The second tab shows the NeurIPS 2025 Datasets & Benchmarks track Call for Papers (in 2026 this track is renamed the **Evaluations & Datasets** track; more on that in a moment), which asks for something different from the main track: "high-quality publications on highly valuable machine learning datasets and benchmarks." Mei has spent the past fourteen months building *both*: a large-scale benchmark of 15,000 hand-annotated multilingual reasoning questions spanning 40 languages, *and* a novel scoring algorithm that correlates better with human judgments than any existing metric. Her benchmark is a substantial research contribution. Her algorithm is algorithmic innovation. The question gnawing at her is deceptively simple: does she write one paper or two?

Her labmate, Aditya, leans over from the next desk. "Just put the benchmark in the appendix of the algorithm paper," he says, tapping the main track CFP. "That's what everyone does. The reviewers want to see that your metric beats the baselines. The benchmark is just the playground." Mei's advisor, Professor Liu, disagrees. She pulls up the NeurIPS 2021 announcement blog post for the Datasets & Benchmarks track and reads aloud: "Work on datasets and benchmarks has been *undervalued, unsupported, and taken for granted*, even though it is crucial for the development and continuous improvement of machine learning methods." She slides her laptop across the table. "Your benchmark is a separate paper. And it might be the more impactful one."

Who is right? The answer requires understanding something that most ML researchers learn too late: the academic publication ecosystem has evolved to recognize different *kinds* of contributions. Forcing a data contribution into an algorithms venue is like submitting a novel to a poetry journal. It might contain beautiful prose, but it will be judged by the wrong criteria. The system is not designed to see its value. This chapter exists to help you see what the system sees, and to write papers that speak its language.

But the stakes are higher than career strategy. Mei's benchmark, if published well, could become the standard evaluation suite for multilingual reasoning. Hundreds of researchers could use it to evaluate their own models, identify weaknesses in particular languages, and track progress over time. If she buries it in an appendix, it will be invisible: a footnote that nobody cites, nobody downloads, and nobody builds on. If she publishes it as a standalone Datasets & Benchmarks paper (with proper documentation, hosted data, baseline experiments, and a clear articulation of what gap it fills), it could shape the research agenda for years. ImageNet ([Deng et al., CVPR 2009](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/5206848)) was published as a dataset paper. SQuAD ([Rajpurkar et al., EMNLP 2016](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.05250)) was published as a dataset paper. SWE-bench ([Jimenez et al., ICLR 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06770)) was published as a benchmark paper. These are among the most-cited works in all of machine learning and natural language processing, not because they introduced clever algorithms, but because they *defined the problems* that clever algorithms would spend years solving.

This chapter guides you through the full picture: what D&B papers are, how they differ from Research papers and System Demo papers, what makes a strong contribution, and how to write one. Each section revisits Dr. Chen's dilemma to provide concrete, grounded examples. By the end, you will understand why her benchmark is indeed a separate paper, what it needs to contain, and how to frame it for the NeurIPS D&B track. You will also understand why the entire ML community has decided that data work deserves its own venue, and why that decision matters more than ever in an era of large language models, autonomous agents, and benchmark contamination.

The figure below plots official NeurIPS conference statistics where available: the [NeurIPS 2023 fact sheet](https://media.neurips.cc/Conferences/NeurIPS2023/NeurIPS2023-Fact_Sheet.pdf) reports **987** Datasets & Benchmarks submissions that year and states the prior year (2022) had **487** submissions; the [NeurIPS 2024 fact sheet](https://media.neurips.cc/Conferences/NeurIPS2024/NeurIPS2024-Fact_Sheet.pdf) reports **1,820** submissions in 2024. The inaugural-year total **484** comes from the original [NeurIPS 2021 track announcement](https://neuripsconf.medium.com/announcing-the-neurips-2021-datasets-and-benchmarks-track-644e27c1e66c) (not the fact sheet series). Together, these numbers show why Mei's dilemma is now everyone's dilemma: the track is no longer a side room; it is a major submission lane. The same series is shown as a bar chart in @fig-neurips-db-submissions.

::: {.callout-warning title="Common Misconception: 'The benchmark belongs in the appendix of the methods paper'"}
Appendix placement signals that the data is *supporting material* for an algorithmic claim. If the benchmark is a general-purpose evaluation resource (new tasks, protocol, baselines, and hosted artifacts), reviewers in a methods track may ask for algorithmic novelty the work does not aim to provide. A dedicated Datasets & Benchmarks or Evaluations & Datasets submission puts the artifact at the center of the review criteria, which is what Mei needs for a 15,000-item multilingual suite intended for community reuse.
:::


### Chapter Introduction {#sec-chapter-intro}

To understand why [**Datasets & Benchmarks**]{style="color: #4F46E5;"} papers exist as a distinct category, you need to appreciate a fundamental asymmetry in how machine learning research has historically been valued. For the better part of two decades, prestige, citations, and career advancement in ML and NLP flowed through a single channel: algorithmic novelty. The incentive structure was clear. You took an existing benchmark (say, GLUE for natural language understanding, or ImageNet for image classification), proposed a new model, a new training procedure, or a new architectural modification, and showed that it achieved state-of-the-art results. The paper that *created* GLUE ([Wang et al., ICLR 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.07461)) was certainly cited, but it was cited as infrastructure, as something you used on the way to your real contribution: the model. The researchers who built GLUE, who designed the tasks, who curated the evaluation data, who built the leaderboard, who maintained the dataset over years? Their work was "service" work, not "research" work, in the eyes of the community.

This asymmetry had consequences. Dataset papers were difficult to publish because they did not fit the review criteria of algorithm-focused venues. Reviewers trained to ask "Where is the algorithmic novelty?" would judge a meticulous dataset curation effort by a standard it was never designed to meet. Benchmark papers fared slightly better. A new benchmark at least *defined* a task, which research culture recognized as valuable. However, even benchmark papers were often relegated to workshop papers or low-prestige venues. The people building the infrastructure on which the entire field depended were being systematically underrewarded for their work.

The turning point came in April 2021, when NeurIPS [announced the creation of a dedicated Datasets & Benchmarks track](https://neuripsconf.medium.com/announcing-the-neurips-2021-datasets-and-benchmarks-track-644e27c1e66c). The announcement was unusually blunt for an academic conference. It stated that work on datasets and benchmarks had been "undervalued, unsupported, and taken for granted"; strong language that acknowledged an institutional failure. The track aimed to make data work "first-class work on par with algorithms work," published in the main NeurIPS proceedings alongside research papers and given its own best-paper awards. The inaugural year received 484 submissions and accepted 174 papers. Among the early highlights were LAION-5B ([Schuhmann et al., NeurIPS 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.08402)), a dataset of 5.85 billion image-text pairs that would go on to enable Stable Diffusion, and MineDojo ([Fan et al., NeurIPS 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.08853)), a Minecraft-based benchmark for open-ended embodied AI that gave the reinforcement learning community an entirely new evaluation paradigm.

The growth since then has been striking. The inaugural year saw **484** submissions ([NeurIPS 2021 track announcement](https://neuripsconf.medium.com/announcing-the-neurips-2021-datasets-and-benchmarks-track-644e27c1e66c)). NeurIPS then integrated the track into the main conference proceedings. Official conference fact sheets report **487** D&B submissions in 2022 (cited as the prior year in the [NeurIPS 2023 fact sheet](https://media.neurips.cc/Conferences/NeurIPS2023/NeurIPS2023-Fact_Sheet.pdf)), **987** in 2023, and **1,820** in 2024 ([NeurIPS 2024 fact sheet](https://media.neurips.cc/Conferences/NeurIPS2024/NeurIPS2024-Fact_Sheet.pdf)): roughly a **4×** jump from 2021 to 2024. Acceptance rates for the track are competitive but not fixed: the same fact sheets report a **32.6%** acceptance rate for D&B in 2023 and **25.3%** in 2024, so the lane is selective even as volume grows. Best-paper winners have included ClimSim ([Yu et al., NeurIPS 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.08754)), a dataset of 5.7 billion multivariate pairs for hybrid physics-ML climate emulation; DecodingTrust ([Wang et al., NeurIPS 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.11698)), a benchmark for evaluating GPT's trustworthiness across multiple safety dimensions; and PRISM ([Kirk et al., NeurIPS 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16019)), a participatory dataset spanning 75 countries for studying multicultural alignment in RLHF. These are not supplementary contributions. They are research artifacts that have shaped entire subfields.

The NeurIPS D&B track was a catalyst, not an endpoint. The broader research community has followed suit. In 2025, [KDD launched its own Datasets & Benchmarks track](https://kdd2025.kdd.org/call-for-datasets-and-benchmarks-track-papers/) for the first time, recognizing that data mining research also depends on high-quality evaluation infrastructure. The [Journal of Data-centric Machine Learning Research (DMLR)](https://dmlr.ai/), a new journal in the JMLR family, launched in October 2023 specifically to provide an archival home for data-focused ML research. Its inaugural volume included a paper titled "Building Better Datasets: Seven Recommendations," an explicit codification of what makes data work excellent. ACL, EMNLP, and NAACL do not have separate D&B tracks, but their reviewer guidelines now explicitly state that "development of datasets is as important as modeling work," and dataset resource papers are a recognized submission category within the main track. The [ACL Rolling Review (ARR) reviewer tutorial](https://aclrollingreview.org/reviewertutorial) makes a formal distinction between "artifact contributions" (datasets, systems, and tools: things you can download and use) and "knowledge contributions" (findings, theories, and algorithms: things you learn from reading). D&B papers are artifact contributions, and the review criteria reflect this.

Starting with NeurIPS 2026, the conference renames the track to [**Evaluations & Datasets**](https://neurips.cc/Conferences/2026/CallForEvaluationsDatasets) and explicitly broadens its mission. The call states that **evaluation becomes an object of scientific study in its own right**: the track welcomes analyses of benchmark failure modes, reproduction and stress-testing of prior evaluations, methodological papers on metrics and protocols, documentation templates for evaluative claims (data cards, model cards, evaluation cards), and critical or negative results about evaluation practices, in addition to the dataset- and benchmark-creation work the track always accepted. Dataset submissions remain central, but authors are asked to spell out the **evaluative role** of the resource: what claims it supports, under what assumptions, and what limitations apply. This shift matters for how you write the paper, not just where you submit it. A contribution that primarily asks "Is this benchmark measuring what we think it measures?" can be a first-class NeurIPS track paper in 2026, whereas in earlier years it might have been a harder fit.

So what, precisely, *is* a Datasets & Benchmarks paper? At its core, a D&B paper is a publication whose [**primary contribution is a data artifact or evaluation infrastructure**]{style="color: #047857;"}, rather than a new algorithm, method, or theoretical result. The [NeurIPS 2025 call for papers](https://neurips.cc/Conferences/2025/CallForDatasetsBenchmarks) lays out the scope explicitly. Acceptable submissions include: new datasets; new benchmarks (with formal evaluation protocols, metrics, and baseline results); data generators and RL environments (such as simulation environments for training and testing agents); data-centric AI tools (for data labeling, curation, cleaning, and quality assessment); data curation practices (novel methodologies for collecting, annotating, or validating data); dataset audits (analyses of existing datasets for bias, quality, representativeness); and competition analyses (post-hoc analyses of machine learning challenge results). KDD's 2025 scope is similar, adding emphasis on data integration and temporal/spatial data. The unifying thread is that *the data or evaluation artifact is the star of the paper*, not a supporting actor.

This distinction is critical because it changes what reviewers look for. When a reviewer evaluates a research paper, they ask: "Does this advance the state of the art in terms of algorithmic performance, theoretical understanding, or empirical insight?" When a reviewer evaluates a D&B paper, they ask a different set of questions: "Is this dataset high-quality, well-documented, and accessible? Does this benchmark test something meaningful that existing benchmarks don't? Will the community use this? Is it ethically sourced and responsibly documented?" A dataset paper that introduces no new algorithm but provides the first large-scale, high-quality evaluation suite for a critical capability (say, multilingual reasoning in 40 languages) is a strong D&B contribution. A research paper that introduces a new algorithm and also releases a small dataset as a side contribution is a strong *research* contribution. The dataset is useful but ancillary. The venue should match the contribution.

The distinction extends to practical submission requirements. For **NeurIPS 2025 and earlier**, D&B papers were *single-blind*, meaning authors were visible to reviewers. The rationale was that dataset and benchmark work often requires verifying that the data is actually hosted, accessible, and of the claimed quality, which is harder to do anonymously. **NeurIPS 2026 changes this default:** the Evaluations & Datasets track is **double-blind by default**, while authors whose submission centers on a dataset may still **opt into single-blind** review. See @sec-track-comparison for the full picture. Since 2025, NeurIPS has required D&B-style submissions to include [Croissant](https://mlcommons.org/working-groups/data/croissant/) metadata (a machine-readable dataset description format supported by HuggingFace, Kaggle, OpenML, and Dataverse) and to host new datasets on a permanent platform. The 2026 call additionally asks authors to complete **Responsible AI (RAI) fields** in Croissant where applicable. Papers that fail to provide accessible data at review time face desk rejection. This is stricter enforcement than the main track, which still allows "code available upon request" in many cases.

For Dr. Chen, this picture is clarifying. Her multilingual reasoning benchmark (15,000 annotated questions across 40 languages, with a formal evaluation protocol, inter-annotator agreement metrics, and baseline experiments from frontier models) is precisely the kind of contribution the D&B track was created to value. It is not an appendix. It is not a footnote. It is a first-class research contribution that fills a specific gap in the evaluation infrastructure for multilingual AI. She will submit it to the NeurIPS Evaluations & Datasets track (formerly Datasets & Benchmarks), host it on HuggingFace with Croissant metadata, and write the paper with the data artifact at center stage. Meanwhile, her scoring algorithm (the novel metric that correlates better with human judgment) will go to the NeurIPS main track or to EMNLP, where reviewers will evaluate it on its algorithmic merits. Two contributions, two papers, two appropriate venues. Neither is diminished by the separation; both are strengthened.

The rest of this chapter walks through the details. @sec-track-comparison provides a thorough comparison of D&B papers, Research papers, and System Demo papers: what each track values, how review criteria differ, and how to decide which track is right for your work. @sec-anatomy-dataset dissects the canonical structure of a dataset paper, from the introduction to the ethics statement, with worked examples from best-paper winners. @sec-anatomy-benchmark does the same for benchmark papers, including Ofir Press's influential framework of three properties that every strong benchmark should have (natural, automatically evaluatable, challenging) and the pressing challenge of benchmark contamination. @sec-why-db-matters steps back to explain why D&B work has become more critical than ever in 2023–2026, driven by LLM benchmark saturation, agentic AI evaluation gaps, and the data-centric AI paradigm shift. Finally, @sec-how-to-write provides a practical guide to writing a competitive D&B submission, including submission logistics, writing tips, common rejection reasons, and a worked example of a complete submission package.

Throughout these sections, we return to Dr. Chen's journey. Each section applies its concepts to her multilingual reasoning benchmark, gradually transforming her initial dilemma into a concrete, well-structured submission. By the end, you will not only understand the D&B field; you will know how to work within it.


### Learning Objectives

After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

- **Distinguish** Datasets & Benchmarks / Evaluations & Datasets papers from Research papers and System Demo papers in terms of what constitutes the primary contribution, how review criteria differ, and which venue is appropriate for which type of work
- **Identify** the map of venues that accept data and evaluation work (NeurIPS Evaluations & Datasets track from 2026 onward, historically Datasets & Benchmarks; KDD D&B track; ACL/EMNLP main track resource papers; DMLR journal) and their specific requirements
- **Structure** a dataset paper using the canonical template: motivation, data collection methodology, documentation, baseline experiments, ethical considerations
- **Design** a benchmark following the three properties of a strong benchmark: natural tasks, automatic evaluability, and calibrated difficulty
- **Articulate** why D&B work is becoming more critical in the LLM and agentic AI era, including the evaluation crisis, benchmark contamination, and the data-centric AI paradigm
- **Prepare** a competitive D&B / Evaluations & Datasets submission including the paper, hosted dataset, Croissant metadata (including RAI fields when required), baseline code, and ethics statement
- **Explain** how formal benchmark-quality frameworks (for example lifecycle-based checklists and community assessments) complement practitioner design heuristics such as Ofir Press's three properties

### Notation

This chapter is primarily conceptual and does not involve heavy mathematical notation. However, a few terms and abbreviations will appear repeatedly:

| Symbol / Abbreviation | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **D&B** | Datasets & Benchmarks (the track/paper type) | "The NeurIPS D&B track" |
| **κ** (kappa) | Cohen's kappa or Fleiss' kappa, inter-annotator agreement metrics | κ = 0.78 indicates "substantial agreement" |
| **α** (alpha) | Krippendorff's alpha, another inter-annotator agreement metric | α > 0.67 is typically the minimum for reliable annotation |
| **pass@k** | Probability that at least one of *k* generated code samples passes all test cases | pass@1 = 0.12 means 12% of single-attempt generations are correct |
| **IAA** | Inter-annotator agreement | "The IAA for our dataset was κ = 0.82" |
| ***CL venues** | ACL, EMNLP, NAACL, COLING, EACL (computational linguistics conferences) | "System demo papers at *CL venues" |
| **CFP** | Call for Papers | "Check the CFP for submission guidelines" |


::: {.exercise-mcq correct="B"}

Dr. Mei's **15,000-question multilingual reasoning suite** with a formal protocol and hosted splits is ready, and she also has a **new scoring algorithm**. Following this chapter's track logic, what is the best first move for the **benchmark** contribution?

- Fold everything into one NeurIPS main-track paper so reviewers see the metric and the data together
- Treat the benchmark as a primary Evaluations & Datasets / D&B submission and the metric as a separate Research submission when it is mature
- Submit the benchmark only as an ACL System Demo because it includes a Gradio tool
- Publish the benchmark as a blog post and cite it from the algorithm paper

::: {.feedback-correct}
Correct. When the main value is the **evaluation artifact** (data + protocol + baselines + hosting), it matches D&B / Evaluations & Datasets criteria. A novel metric is a **knowledge** contribution reviewed as methods work in the main track.
:::

::: {.feedback-incorrect}
Not quite. The benchmark is an **artifact contribution** judged on usefulness, documentation, and accessibility. The main track centers **algorithmic novelty**. Splitting routes each piece to the right reviewers. Combining everything forces one set of reviewers to use the wrong rubric, and burying the benchmark in an appendix undermines its visibility.
:::

:::


::: {.exercise-predict correct="C"}

You have read that NeurIPS Datasets & Benchmarks was **single-blind** through 2025. Before checking your memory of the **2026 Evaluations & Datasets** call: what is the **default** review mode for that track?

- Single-blind for every submission, unchanged from 2025
- Open review with public identities during the whole process
- Double-blind by default, with an opt-in for single-blind when the submission centers on releasing a dataset

::: {.predict-reveal}
**The answer is C.** NeurIPS 2026 broadens scope to evaluation science, so the default shifts to **double-blind**; authors whose work **centers on a dataset** may still **choose single-blind** when anonymizing the release is impractical. If you picked single-blind for all, you were extrapolating the old default without the 2026 carve-out.
:::

:::
